summary: Converting tenths to hundredths rests on place value and the equivalent-fraction principle (×10/×10): one tenth is ten hundredths, so 3/10 = 30/100, and 3/10 + 4/100 becomes 30/100 + 4/100 = 34/100. Learners cannot combine tenths and hundredths until the pieces are the same size, so the conversion must happen before adding. A 10×10 hundredths grid (each column = one tenth = ten small squares) makes this relationship concrete; a base-ten flat/rod model, place-value columns, number lines, money (£0.30 = 30p) and metric (3/10 m = 30 cm) anchor it in familiar units, and the decimal form (34/100 = 0.34) bridges to decimal notation.
misconceptions: Adds across both denominators: 3/10 + 4/100 = 7/110 (adds tops and bottoms)
Treats 3/10 as 3 hundredths, shading three single squares, and reports 7/100
Thinks the denominators can be added because 'they are close', ignoring that the pieces are different sizes

activities.title: Build 3/10 + 4/100 on a hundredths grid
steps: Take a blank 10×10 hundredths grid where each full column of ten small squares represents one tenth.
Shade 3/10 by filling three whole columns, then count the small squares covered to confirm it is 30 hundredths.
Add 4/100 by shading four more single squares.
Count all the shaded small squares and report the total as hundredths (34/100), then, when ready, write it as a decimal (0.34).
Deliberately try shading just three lone single squares for 3/10 first, notice that this is only 3/100, then correct it to three full columns.

Optionally model the same amounts with base-ten blocks, where the flat is one whole, a rod is one tenth, and a small cube is one hundredth, to see the same ×10 relationship in a different manipulative.
activities.insight: Three tenths covers the same shaded area as thirty hundredths, so tenths must be converted to hundredths before they can be added to hundredths.

activities.title: Explain why 5/10 = 50/100 and challenge the 7/110 error
steps: On a hundredths grid, show 5/10 and explain why it covers 50 small squares, not 5.
Rewrite 7/10 as an equivalent fraction over 100 (70/100).
Respond to a classmate who claims 3/10 + 4/100 = 7/110: explain out loud why you never add the denominators, using the idea that the pieces are different sizes until converted.
When offered answer choices such as 34/100, 7/110 and 7/100, pick 34/100 and say explicitly why each of the other two is wrong.
Sort several sums into 'already hundredths' versus 'convert a tenth first' before solving them.
activities.insight: Equivalent tenths-to-hundredths conversions come from multiplying numerator and denominator by ten; denominators are never added because they name the size of the pieces, which must match before combining.

activities.title: Connect to place value, money and metric, then to decimals
steps: Place tenths and hundredths into a place-value chart with labelled tenths and hundredths columns and read the conversion from the columns.
Match each fraction to a familiar unit: 3/10 = £0.30 = 30p, and 3/10 m = 30 cm, noting the ×10 relationship.
Mark 0.34 on a 0–1 number line divided into hundredths and relate it to 34/100.
Write a converted answer such as 34/100 as the decimal 0.34 and say why they are the same quantity.
Transfer to a fresh pair, e.g. 6/10 + 7/100 (= 67/100), aiming to convert without needing the grid.
activities.insight: The tenth-to-hundredth ×10 relationship is the same structure seen in place value, money and metric measures, and it bridges directly to decimal notation.

checkQuestion: Put a blank 10×10 hundredths grid in front of the child. Say: 'Show me 3/10 on this grid, then show me 4/100 as well, and tell me how much you have altogether written as hundredths.' Then watch — say nothing about how to do it.
checkAnswer: Shades three full columns for 3/10 (recognising that is 30 small squares / 30 hundredths), adds four single squares for 4/100, and reports 34/100 (may also say 0.34).
